newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Warring Russian tycoon turns to Yeltsin, court.
newsitem.headline: Warring Russian tycoon turns to Yeltsin, court.

text.p: The feud that has broken out among business tycoons with links to the Kremlin turned uglier on Thursday with one media magnate suing a rival and suggesting the uproar could bring down young reformers in the government.

Reform chief Anatoly Chubais, 42, tried to cool tempers on Wednesday, saying President Boris Yeltsin was satisfied with the sale of a quarter of state telecoms company Svyazinvest to a consortium led by a 36-year-old banker and former minister and backed by U.S. financier George Soros.

Instead the feud simmered away on Thursday when a businessman widely named by political and industry sources as a key player in the losing bid launched a slander suit against the leader of the winning consortium for suggesting he tried to mount a "backroom deal".

A spokesman for media and banking tycoon Vladimir Gusinsky, who read out a statement announcing his suit, also stoked the political temperature by hinting Yeltsin could and should act "firmly" against the liberal ministers who supported the sale.
"As a result of the scandal...cracks have appeared in the face of the government," Gusinsky's spokesman Vyacheslav Kostikov, once Yeltsin's own spokesman, told a news conference.

He praised a move by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to study the Svyazinvest sale more closely, arguing the buyers were foreign speculators who were in cahoots with top ministers. He said the 58-year-old premier, believed to be less keen on rapid reforms than Chubais, shared Gusinsky's concerns over the deal.

"I don't rule out that one of the activists, whom we've seen recently on our screens, might find themselves experiencing an unintential and unforeseen loneliness," Kostikov said, in an apparent reference to liberal ministers like Boris Nemtsov, 37.

Some leading business groups, through the newspapers and television channels they control, have lambasted the sale, which was the country's biggest ever privatisation. They have accused Nemtsov, a first deputy premier and golden boy of reforms, as well as other liberals, of colluding with the winning bidders.

The auction winner, Uneximbank chief Vladimir Potanin, says the criticism is just sour grapes on the part of Gusinsky, who controls the Most banking and media empire, and another tycoon, Boris Berezovsky, currently a senior Kremlin security official.

Top government sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, corroborate Potanin's account that all three -- Potanin, Gusinsky and Berezovsky -- had flown to France last week to try to agree the outcome of the auction in advance with Chubais.

Gusinsky's spokesman said the Most group took no part in the losing bid, whose backers have not been officially identified. But he added that he had "no information" when asked if Gusinsky attended the meeting involving Potanin, Berezovsky and Chubais.

Chubais has spearheaded Russia's post-Soviet privatisation drive since the early 1990s, while Nemtsov, a reformist provincial leader, was brought to Moscow by Yeltsin in March to clean up the government.

They say the Svyazinvest auction marks a break with past backroom carve-ups of state assets among the business groups which rallied their money and media muscle behind Yeltsin's re-election campaign last year.
Financial analysts welcomed the deal for being competitive and valuing Svyazinvest at a price close to its real worth.
Political sources say Chubais is now seeking the maximum amount of cash for the treasury from assets sales.
Gusinsky's spokesman noted, however, that the fallout from the row was as much about politics as commerce.

Behind all the manoeuvring, some Kremlin sources say, lie struggles within the establishment for the mantle of Yeltsin's heir. Sources say Chubais, a kingmaker rather than a contender himself, is rallying support around the telegenic Nemtsov.
Gusinsky's spokesman raised the question of whether Chubais and others close to Yeltsin, who is 66 and carrying a multiple heart bypass, were preparing for an early election.

"Does this group of very hurried young people know something about our president, Boris Nikolayevich, which we don't?" Kostikov said. "Maybe, these people...have seen something in his eyes? Something that's making them hurry the course of the events, laid down in the constitution for the year 2000?"
Kostikov, known for his shoot-from-the-hip style during his days in the Kremlin, said he believed Yeltsin would react to the "scandal" by proving he is "a strong, firm politician".
